components.note: 口 (mouth) — 号 relates to calling or crying out aloud, as well as a spoken or marked sign
丂 gives a loose sound connection to 号's reading hào
石 (stone) — 码 originally related to counting stones used for reckoning, extended to mean 'number, code.'
马 (mǎ) is an exact match for the sound of 码.

example.hanzi: 你的电话号码是多少?
example.pinyin: Nǐ de diànhuà hàomǎ shì duōshao?
example.english: What's your phone number?
example.fact: 号码 names an identifying number treated as a label — a phone number, room number, ID number — while 数字 is reserved for digits or figures used in counting and math; reaching for 数字 to ask someone's phone number is a common learner mix-up.

components.note: 日 depicts the sun as a circle with a dot or short stroke inside — a simplified picture of the sun's disc, later squared off in the standard script.
A simple drawing of a swaddled baby — arms reaching out, legs bundled together in a wrap.

example.hanzi: 他们过着幸福的日子。
example.pinyin: Tāmen guòzhe xìngfú de rìzi.
example.english: They are living a happy life.
example.fact: 日子 stretches beyond a single calendar date to mean "the days of one's life," which is why 过日子 (guò rìzi, literally "to pass one's days") is the everyday idiom for "to get by" or "to live one's life" — a sense the more literal 天 ("day," as a count) doesn't carry.

components.note: 比 is made of two identical 匕 (spoon) shapes placed side by side — comparing two similar things led to its meaning 'to compare.'
女 (woman) — depicts a wife in the traditional image behind this character.
口 (mouth/words) — the wife following her husband's spoken words gave 如 its meaning of 'as, like, if.'

example.hanzi: 很多水果都很甜,比如西瓜和芒果。
example.pinyin: Hěnduō shuǐguǒ dōu hěn tián, bǐrú xīguā hé mángguǒ.
example.english: Many fruits are sweet, for example watermelon and mango.
example.fact: 比如 sits at the conversational end of Chinese's "for example" words — its cousin 例如 carries the same meaning but leans more formal and written, useful to know when picking the right register for giving an example.

components.note: 口 (mouth) — used when asking a question aloud
那 (nà) gives a sound close to 哪's reading nǎ, differing mainly in tone
丨 (a vertical tally mark) over 人 (person) — suggests counting people one by one, fitting 个's role today as Mandarin's most common general measure word.

example.hanzi: 这两件衬衫,你喜欢哪个?
example.pinyin: Zhè liǎng jiàn chènshān, nǐ xǐhuan nǎge?
example.english: Of these two shirts, which one do you like?
example.fact: 哪个 pairs the question word 哪 ("which") with 个, Mandarin's default measure word — the same "question word + 个" pattern behind 这个/那个 elsewhere in this deck — though a more specific classifier (哪件, 哪本) is used when the noun calls for one.

components.note: 刂 (knife) — 剩 originally involved cutting away a surplus portion, giving 'to remain, leftover.'
乘 (chéng) shares the rhyme -eng and a related retroflex initial (ch/sh) with shèng — only the tone differs.
A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 蛋糕吃了一半,剩下的放冰箱里。
example.pinyin: Dàngāo chīle yíbàn, shèngxià de fàng bīngxiāng lǐ.
example.english: Half the cake got eaten; put what's left in the fridge.
example.fact: 剩下 is a verb plus result-complement: 剩 alone already means "to be left over," and 下 adds a sense of settling or remaining in place — the same verb + 下 pattern seen in 留下 ("to leave behind") and 坐下 ("to sit down").

components.note: 千 (thousand) — 重 pictures a heavy burden carried a great distance.
里 (a unit of distance, like a mile) — carrying something a thousand 里 emphasizes how heavy and significant a burden it is, giving 重 its meaning 'heavy' or 'important.'

example.hanzi: 这次交通事故很严重。
example.pinyin: Zhè cì jiāotōng shìgù hěn yánzhòng.
example.english: This traffic accident was very serious.
example.fact: 严重 describes how grave a problem, illness, or situation is, but never a person's manner or personality — for a "serious" demeanor, Chinese instead reaches for 严肃, a split that English's single word "serious" glosses over.

components.note: 亠 (a roof) — the top of a house.
口 (a mouth) — eating and enjoying inside it.
子 (a child) — together showing a family living and eating well under one roof, giving 享 its meaning 'to enjoy.'
爫 (a hand, from above) — 受 pictures something being passed.
又 (a hand, from below) — one hand giving and another receiving gave 受 its meaning 'to receive' or 'to endure.'

example.hanzi: 周末我喜欢在家享受安静的时光。
example.pinyin: Zhōumò wǒ xǐhuan zài jiā xiǎngshòu ānjìng de shíguāng.
example.english: On weekends I like to enjoy quiet time at home.
example.fact: 享 alone means "to partake of, to be granted" and 受 alone means "to receive" — together 享受 frames enjoyment as something received and savored rather than something actively chased, a gentler image than the more effortful 追求 ("to pursue").

components.note: 戈 (a dagger-axe, a weapon) — 战 relates to fighting and war.
占 (zhàn) gives the sound — 战 is also pronounced zhàn, an exact match.
爪 and 彐 (two hands, reaching from opposite sides) — a simplified form of 爭, grabbing for the same thing.
亅 (the object) — what the two hands are struggling over, giving 争 its meaning 'to contend, compete, fight for.'

example.hanzi: 这部电影讲述了一场战争的故事。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng jiǎngshùle yì chǎng zhànzhēng de gùshi.
example.english: This movie tells the story of a war.
example.fact: 战争 takes the measure word 场 (chǎng), the same classifier used for large-scale events like sports matches and rainstorms — a reminder that Chinese measure words often group nouns by scale or shape rather than by category.

components.note: Heart — respect and politeness are expressed from the heart.
Gives the sound gòng, related to gōng but drifted apart over time.
壴 (a drum) — beating a drum in celebration
口 (mouth) — singing along in celebration

example.hanzi: 恭喜你考上了大学!
example.pinyin: Gōngxǐ nǐ kǎoshàngle dàxué!
example.english: Congratulations on getting into university!
example.fact: 恭喜 anchors the standard Chinese New Year greeting 恭喜发财 ("congratulations, may you prosper") — one of the clearest everyday windows into 恭喜's specifically celebratory, good-news register, distinct from a plain politeness word.

components.note: 乂 depicts crossed strokes suggesting a cutting action.
木 (wood) here represents a wooden stake — giving 杀 its meaning 'to kill.'
匕 (a kneeling person) — a mourner bowed down in grief.
歹 (skeletal remains) — the corpse being mourned, the source of 死's meaning 'to die, dead.'

example.hanzi: 医生想办法杀死癌细胞。
example.pinyin: Yīshēng xiǎng bànfǎ shāsǐ ái xìbāo.
example.english: Doctors look for ways to kill cancer cells.
example.fact: Adding 死 after 杀 makes the killing's outcome explicit — 杀 alone can describe an attack without confirming the target actually died — placing 杀死 in a family of verb + 死 resultative compounds that includes 淹死 ("to drown") and 冻死 ("to freeze to death").

components.note: 彡 (fine lines) — suggests light and shadow, relating to 影's meaning 'shadow, image.'
景 (jǐng) gives a sound hint — 影 is pronounced yǐng, sharing the same rhyme though the initial consonant differs.
口 (mouth) — 响 relates to sound, something that can be heard
向 (xiàng) gives a loose sound connection to 响's reading xiǎng

example.hanzi: 睡眠不足会影响你的健康。
example.pinyin: Shuìmián bùzú huì yǐngxiǎng nǐ de jiànkāng.
example.english: Lack of sleep can affect your health.
example.fact: 影响 literally pairs "shadow" (影) with "echo" (响) — two things that trail an original cause without ever touching it directly, a fitting image behind a word that describes an effect propagating outward from its source.

components.note: 禾 (grain, a growing rice or wheat plant) — 利 pictures a harvest.
刂 (knife) — cutting grain at harvest time was a clear benefit or gain, giving 利 its meaning 'profit' or 'advantage.'

example.hanzi: 他利用假期学习了法语。
example.pinyin: Tā lìyòng jiàqī xuéxíle Fǎyǔ.
example.english: He made use of his vacation to study French.
example.fact: 利用 can describe resourcefully making the most of something (利用假期, "made use of the vacation") or exploiting someone in a self-serving way (利用别人, "to use/exploit someone") — one word covers both the neutral-positive and the negative sense, and only context decides which.

components.note: 乂 depicts crossed strokes suggesting a cutting action.
木 (wood) here represents a wooden stake — giving 杀 its meaning 'to kill.'
A simple line drawing of a person's legs seen from the side, used to depict a human being.

example.hanzi: 警方正在调查一起杀人案。
example.pinyin: Jǐngfāng zhèngzài diàochá yì qǐ shārén àn.
example.english: Police are investigating a murder case.
example.fact: 杀人 is a verb-object compound (杀 "to kill" + 人 "person") loose enough to still take material worked in, as in 杀人犯 ("murderer," literally "kill-person offender") — a flexibility that a fully fused synonym like 谋杀 ("to murder") doesn't share.

components.note: 丿 (something falling) — an object slipping away.
夫 (a hand/person) — the object slipping out of a hand, giving 失 its meaning 'to lose.'
足 (foot) — 踪 names the footprints or tracks left behind.
宗 (zōng) gives the sound — an exact match with 踪.

example.hanzi: 那艘船在海上失踪了。
example.pinyin: Nà sōu chuán zài hǎishàng shīzōng le.
example.english: That ship went missing at sea.
example.fact: 踪 on its own means "tracks, traces" (as in 踪迹, "footprints, trace") — so 失踪 literally means "to lose one's tracks," painting someone vanishing so completely that not even a trail remains, the vivid image behind the everyday word for "missing."

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 认 relates to recognizing or acknowledging something, often expressed through words.
人 (rén) gives the sound — 认 is pronounced rèn, a close variant of the same sound.
直 (straight, upright) — 真 relates to something level and true.
几 (a small table) — an object placed level and true on a table gave 真 its meaning 'real' or 'true.'

example.hanzi: 他工作一直很认真。
example.pinyin: Tā gōngzuò yìzhí hěn rènzhēn.
example.english: He has always been very conscientious in his work.
example.fact: 认真 usually describes an attitude toward doing a specific task carefully (认真学习, "study earnestly") rather than a fixed personality trait, sitting closer to English "diligent" or "earnest" than to 严重's problem-focused "serious" (also in this batch), even though dictionaries sometimes gloss both as "serious."

components.note: 直 (straight, upright) — 真 relates to something level and true.
几 (a small table) — an object placed level and true on a table gave 真 its meaning 'real' or 'true.'
木 (tree) — 相 pictures looking closely at a tree.
目 (eye) — staring closely at a tree to examine it gave 相 the meaning 'to observe' or, later, 'each other, mutual.'

example.hanzi: 记者们想找出事件的真相。
example.pinyin: Jìzhěmen xiǎng zhǎochū shìjiàn de zhēnxiàng.
example.english: The reporters wanted to find out the truth behind the incident.
example.fact: 真相 specifically names a hidden or underlying truth waiting to be uncovered — the reason it shows up constantly in detective stories and scandal reporting — rather than a plain factual statement, which is why the set phrase 真相大白 ("the truth comes to light") reads almost cinematically.

components.note: 氵 (water/stream) — water naturally follows a fixed course, an image linked to the idea of 'law' or 'method.'
去 (to go/a course) — the path a stream follows suggested a regulated, consistent way of doing things, hence 'law, method.'
彳 (to walk/step) — represents movement or conduct.
聿 (an old form related to a writing brush) — conduct guided by written rules gave 律 its meaning 'law, regulation.'

example.hanzi: 每个人都应该遵守法律。
example.pinyin: Měi gè rén dōu yīnggāi zūnshǒu fǎlǜ.
example.english: Everyone should obey the law.
example.fact: 律 is properly pronounced with the ü umlaut, lǜ — after l and n the dots can never be dropped the way they are after j/q/x/y, since lu/lü and nu/nü are genuinely different syllables (律 lǜ versus, say, 卢 lú) that would otherwise collide.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 训 relates to teaching through spoken instruction.
川 (chuān) gives a sound distantly related to xùn, having drifted apart over time.
纟 (thread) — 练 originally meant to boil and whiten silk thread, extending to 'to practice, to train' through repeated refinement.
柬 (jiǎn) gives a sound distantly related to liàn, having drifted apart over time.

example.hanzi: 运动员每天都要训练。
example.pinyin: Yùndòngyuán měitiān dōu yào xùnliàn.
example.english: Athletes have to train every day.
example.fact: 训 alone means "to instruct" (as in 教训, "lesson, to reprimand") while 练 alone means "to practice, to drill" (as in 练习) — 训练 pairs an instructional half with a practice half, describing guided, structured practice rather than solo repetition.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 值 relates to worth or value assigned by a person
直 (zhí) gives the sound — 值 is also pronounced zhí, an exact match
寸 (a hand) reaching for 旦 (originally 貝, a shell used as currency) — a picture of grasping something valuable, hence 'to obtain, to get.'

example.hanzi: 这部电影很值得一看。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng hěn zhíde yí kàn.
example.english: This movie is well worth watching.
example.fact: 值得 slots directly in front of a verb phrase to mean "worth doing X" (值得一看, "worth watching"; 值得尝试, "worth trying") — a compact construction that English can only match by adding a separate gerund after "worth."

components.note: 月 (yuè) here actually derives from 肉 (meat) — 有 originally depicted a hand holding meat, meaning 'to possess'; it also lends a loose phonetic connection to yǒu.
心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
An altered form of 囟 (the mind/head) — the seat of thought.
心 (heart) — thinking was pictured as an activity of both mind and heart, giving 思 its meaning 'to think.'

example.hanzi: 这本书的故事很有意思。
example.pinyin: Zhè běn shū de gùshi hěn yǒuyìsi.
example.english: The story in this book is very interesting.
example.fact: 有意思 literally combines "to have" (有) with "meaning/interest" (意思) — its negation, casually shortened to 没意思, means "boring, meaningless," the flip side of the same "has/lacks meaning" image.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 使 involves a person carrying out a task.
吏 (a government official) — 使 originally referred to an official sent to carry out orders, giving rise to the meaning 'to make someone do something' or 'to use.'

example.hanzi: 请按照说明使用这台机器。
example.pinyin: Qǐng ànzhào shuōmíng shǐyòng zhè tái jīqì.
example.english: Please use this machine according to the instructions.
example.fact: 使用 is the more formal, often written register for "to use" a tool or method, while everyday spoken Mandarin defaults to the plainer 用 for the same idea — a register gap similar to English "utilize" versus "use."

components.note: 面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'

example.hanzi: 在健康方面,他非常小心。
example.pinyin: Zài jiànkāng fāngmiàn, tā fēicháng xiǎoxīn.
example.english: When it comes to health, he is very careful.
example.fact: 方面 typically follows a noun to frame "in the respect/area of X" (健康方面, "health-wise") — a common sentence-opening move that lets a speaker narrow down which angle of a topic they mean before saying anything else about it.

components.note: 钅 (metal) — 银 refers to silver, a metal
艮 (gèn) gives a sound distantly related to 银's reading yín, having drifted apart over time
彳 depicts a step with the left foot; together with 亍 (a step with the right foot), 行 shows a person walking or moving.
亍 depicts a step with the right foot, complementing 彳 to form the idea of walking or travel.

example.hanzi: 我需要去银行取钱。
example.pinyin: Wǒ xūyào qù yínháng qǔ qián.
example.english: I need to go to the bank to withdraw money.
example.fact: 行 is a classic multi-reading character: pronounced xíng it means "to go, OK, will do" (as in the stand-alone reply 行!, "sure, that works"), but pronounced háng it names an orderly row or a professional trade — the háng reading is the one locked into 银行 ("bank") and 行业 ("industry").

components.note: 心 (heart) — 恐 describes fear felt in the heart.
巩 (gǒng) gives a sound close to kǒng, sharing the same rhyme.
Heart — fear is a feeling in the heart/mind.
Gives the sound bù, matching the character's reading.

example.hanzi: 那部恐怖电影把我吓坏了。
example.pinyin: Nà bù kǒngbù diànyǐng bǎ wǒ xiàhuài le.
example.english: That horror movie scared me badly.
example.fact: 恐怖 reduplicates the idea of fear across both halves — 恐 alone means "to dread" and 怖 alone also means "terrified" — the same intensifying, two-near-synonym structure behind 喜欢 ("to like") elsewhere in this deck; 恐怖片 specifically names the horror-film genre.

meanings: so, actually, as it turns out

components.note: 厂 (a cliff or overhang) — 原 relates to a source high up, such as a spring emerging from rock.
泉 (quán) gives a hint of the sound — 原 is pronounced yuán, a connection that has shifted somewhat.
Originally depicted a wheat plant; this agricultural picture was borrowed early on to represent the unrelated verb 'to come.'

example.hanzi: 我原来打算八点出发,但是迟到了。
example.pinyin: Wǒ yuánlái dǎsuan bā diǎn chūfā, dànshì chídào le.
example.english: I had originally planned to leave at eight, but I ended up being late.
example.fact: Beyond its literal "originally," 原来 doubles as a mid-sentence realization marker meaning "oh, so that's how it is" (原来是这样啊!) — a jump from describing the past to voicing sudden understanding that learners who only memorize the first sense often miss.

components.note: 言 (speech) — 警 relates to speaking out a warning or alarm
敬 (jìng) gives a sound close to 警's reading jǐng, sharing a similar historical pronunciation

example.hanzi: 警官,请帮帮我。
example.pinyin: Jǐngguān, qǐng bāngbang wǒ.
example.english: Officer, please help me.
example.fact: 警官 typically works as a title used to address or refer to an individual police officer by rank, while 警察 is the broader, more common word for "police" as an occupation or institution — roughly the same split as English "officer" versus "police."

components.note: 忄 (heart/mind) — 性 relates to inner nature or character.
生 (shēng) gives a hint of the sound — 性 is pronounced xìng, a related sound though the initial has shifted.
咸 (all, together) — 感 relates to a shared reaction.
心 (heart) — feelings that stir the heart gave 感 its meaning 'to feel' or 'emotion.'

example.hanzi: 她今天穿的裙子很性感。
example.pinyin: Tā jīntiān chuān de qúnzi hěn xìnggǎn.
example.english: The dress she's wearing today is very sexy.
example.fact: 性感 combines 性 ("sex, nature") with 感 ("feeling, sense") — literally "a sexual feeling" — an almost exact structural parallel to how English "sexy" grew out of the noun "sex" plus the adjective-forming "-y."

components.note: A picture of a nose; because people in ancient China would point to their own nose when referring to themselves, the character came to mean 'self.'
乂 depicts crossed strokes suggesting a cutting action.
木 (wood) here represents a wooden stake — giving 杀 its meaning 'to kill.'

example.hanzi: 他因为压力太大而选择了自杀。
example.pinyin: Tā yīnwèi yālì tài dà ér xuǎnzéle zìshā.
example.english: He chose to end his own life because the pressure became too much.
example.fact: 自杀 is a reflexive verb-object compound, literally "self-kill" (自 "self" + 杀 "to kill") — the same reflexive 自- element that opens 自己 ("oneself") and 自我 ("self, ego"), all marking that an action's target is the subject itself.

components.note: 酉 (a wine jar) — the vessel holding the drink
氵 (liquid) — the wine itself inside the jar
口 (mouth) — 吧 is a spoken particle, tied to speech and the mouth
巴 (bā) gives the sound — 吧 is pronounced ba, a related (unstressed) form of the same sound

example.hanzi: 我们晚上去酒吧喝一杯吧。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen wǎnshang qù jiǔbā hē yì bēi ba.
example.english: Let's go to a bar for a drink tonight.
example.fact: 吧 in 酒吧 is a phonetic loan borrowed purely for its sound to render English "bar," not for any meaning of its own — the same borrowed 吧 shows up in 迪吧 (dībā, "disco") and 网吧 (wǎngbā, "internet café"), a small family of "X-bar" loanwords.

components.note: 讠 (speech) — 讨 involves speaking, as in asking or discussing.
寸 (a hand/small measure) — combined with speech, suggests reaching out verbally to ask for something, giving 讨 its meaning 'to ask for, to discuss.'
讠 (speech) — 论 relates to discussing or explaining something with words.
仑 (logical order, arrangement) — combined with speech, 论 came to mean 'to discuss' or 'a theory,' explaining ideas in an orderly way.

example.hanzi: 我们下午要讨论这个计划。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xiàwǔ yào tǎolùn zhège jìhuà.
example.english: We're going to discuss this plan in the afternoon.
example.fact: 讨论 takes its object directly with no preposition needed (讨论这个问题, "discuss this problem") — a common trap for English speakers who reflexively want to add "about" after "discuss," a habit that doesn't carry over into Chinese.

components.note: 凡 (common/ordinary) — suggests something shared or held in common.
口 (mouth) — sharing a common mouth/voice with others gave 同 its meaning of 'same, together.'
木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 我们俩有同样的爱好。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen liǎ yǒu tóngyàng de àihào.
example.english: The two of us have the same hobbies.
example.fact: 同样 usually sits directly before a noun as an attributive ("the same X") or before a clause meaning "likewise," while its near-synonym 一样 (also in this deck) more often follows a comparison frame like "A 跟 B 一样" — both mean "same" but favor different positions in the sentence.

components.note: 身 depicts a person's torso, originally showing a pregnant woman's body — later broadened to mean 'the body' in general.
亻 (person) — the person receiving a share
分 (to divide) — the portion allotted to that person

example.hanzi: 请出示您的身份证。
example.pinyin: Qǐng chūshì nín de shēnfènzhèng.
example.english: Please show your ID card.
example.fact: 身份 shows up constantly in the compound 身份证 (shēnfènzhèng, literally "identity-proof-certificate") — one of the most important pieces of paperwork in daily life in China, required for everything from buying train tickets to checking into a hotel.

components.note: 讠 (speech radical) — shows 说 relates to talking or language
兑 (duì) is the phonetic component; historically 说 was also pronounced closer to 兑's sound before shifting to shuō
日 (sun) — combined with 月 (moon), 明 shows the light of both sun and moon, giving the meaning 'bright' or 'clear.'
月 (moon) — together with 日 (sun), the two brightest things in the sky represent brightness and clarity.

example.hanzi: 请你说明一下这个规则。
example.pinyin: Qǐng nǐ shuōmíng yíxià zhège guīzé.
example.english: Please explain this rule.
example.fact: 说明 works as both a verb ("to explain, indicate") and a noun ("explanation, instructions"), the noun sense showing up on packaging as 说明书 (shuōmíngshū, "instruction manual") — one word doing double duty across two different English parts of speech.

components.note: 亻 (person) — 什 originally referred to a group of people.
十 (ten) — combined with 亻 (person), 什 originally described a group of ten; the character later came to be used for the common word 什么 (what).
木 (tree/wood) — 样 originally referred to a kind of tree, later broadening to mean 'kind, appearance, way.'
羊 (yáng) gives the sound — 样 is pronounced yàng, matching aside from tone.

example.hanzi: 你想找什么样的工作?
example.pinyin: Nǐ xiǎng zhǎo shénmeyàng de gōngzuò?
example.english: What kind of job are you looking for?
example.fact: 什么样 attaches 样 ("kind, appearance") onto the question word 什么 to ask about type rather than identity, almost always followed by 的 before the noun it modifies — the same "X样" structure behind 这样/那样 elsewhere in this deck, just turned into a question.

components.note: 宀 (a roof, house) — 安 pictures shelter.
女 (woman) — a woman safely inside a house gave 安 its meaning 'peace' or 'safety.'
青 (blue-green, nature) — 静 relates to a calm stillness, like still water or clear skies
争 (zhēng) gives a sound distantly related to 静's reading jìng, having drifted apart over time

example.hanzi: 图书馆里非常安静。
example.pinyin: Túshūguǎn lǐ fēicháng ānjìng.
example.english: It's very quiet inside the library.
example.fact: 安静 describes both an environment free of noise (图书馆很安静, "the library is quiet") and, applied to a person, a calm and undemonstrative temperament (安静的孩子, "a quiet child") — the same word stretching to cover a hushed room and a reserved personality, much like English "quiet."

components.note: 木 (wood) — early models and molds were often carved from wood
莫 (mò) gives a sound close to 模's reading mó, sharing a similar historical pronunciation
牛 (ox) — 特 originally referred to a male ox singled out for sacrifice, a special animal set apart from the herd.
寺 (sì) gives a hint of the sound — 特 is pronounced tè, a connection that has drifted over time.

example.hanzi: 她是一名时装模特。
example.pinyin: Tā shì yì míng shízhuāng mótè.
example.english: She is a fashion model.
example.fact: 模特 is a straightforward phonetic transliteration of English "model," built purely to approximate the foreign sound rather than to carry meaning through its individual characters — the same strategy behind loanwords like 咖啡 (kāfēi, "coffee").

components.note: 夕 (evening/night), doubled — two nights stacked together suggested the idea of accumulation, giving 多 its meaning of 'many, much.'

example.hanzi: 这里的风景多么美丽啊!
example.pinyin: Zhèlǐ de fēngjǐng duōme měilì a!
example.english: How beautiful the scenery here is!
example.fact: 多么 is an exclamatory intensifier that almost always closes its sentence with a particle like 啊 for emotional emphasis (多么...啊!) — a fixed frame that mirrors English "How wonderful it is!", both languages front-loading the intensifier ahead of the adjective.

components.note: 足 depicts a leg (the upper shape) above a foot — a simple picture of the human leg and foot, giving 足 its meaning 'foot, to be sufficient.'
多 (more/many) — 够 relates to having a sufficient amount
句 (jù) gives a loose sound connection to 够's reading gòu

example.hanzi: 我们的食物足够吃一个星期。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen de shíwù zúgòu chī yí gè xīngqī.
example.english: Our food is enough to last a week.
example.fact: 足够 covers the same ground as its shorter, more casual cousin 够 (够了!, "That's enough!") but leans toward the more formal or written end of the register — plain 够 dominates in everyday speech.

components.note: 冖 (a covering/roof) — represents the building or schoolhouse where learning happens.
子 (child) — 学 depicts children gathered to study.
⺍ is a small graphic element at the top of the character; its original pictorial meaning, if any, has been lost over time.
屮 (a young shoot) growing up out of 土 (earth/soil) — a picture of new life emerging from the ground.

example.hanzi: 教室里坐着二十个学生。
example.pinyin: Jiàoshì lǐ zuòzhe èrshí gè xuésheng.
example.english: Twenty students are sitting in the classroom.
example.fact: 生 alone carries the core sense "to be born, to grow, life" (as in 先生, also in this deck) — 学生 literally pairs "study" (学) with that "life/growing" root, framing a student as someone still growing through learning, the same 生 behind 医生 ("doctor") and 陌生 ("unfamiliar").

components.note: A short stroke placed below a longer one — the mirror image of 上 (up), together forming a simple, opposite pair.

example.hanzi: 我们下午三点见面。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen xiàwǔ sān diǎn jiànmiàn.
example.english: Let's meet at three in the afternoon.
example.fact: 午 alone names midday (as in 午饭, "lunch"), and Mandarin builds its whole day-part vocabulary directionally around it: 上午 ("before noon, morning"), 下午 ("after noon, afternoon"), and 中午 ("exactly noon") — a tidy three-way system anchored on a single character.

components.note: 乃 (then, thus) — 仍 relates to continuity, 'still, as before'
亻 gives a loose sound connection to 仍's reading réng
灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 虽然他道歉了,但她仍然很生气。
example.pinyin: Suīrán tā dàoqiànle, dàn tā réngrán hěn shēngqì.
example.english: Even though he apologized, she was still very angry.
example.fact: 仍然 is the fuller, more formal-sounding two-syllable form built by adding 然 onto the shorter adverb 仍 — the same 然-suffixing pattern that produces 忽然 ("suddenly") and 显然 ("obviously") from their own single-syllable roots.

components.note: A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.
日 (the sun) — rising above.
一 (a horizontal line) — the horizon, together giving 旦 its meaning 'dawn, daybreak.'

example.hanzi: 一旦你做出决定,就要坚持下去。
example.pinyin: Yīdàn nǐ zuòchū juédìng, jiù yào jiānchí xiàqù.
example.english: Once you make a decision, you should stick with it.
example.fact: 一旦 keeps its plain number-one tone yī rather than shifting to yí before the 4th-tone 旦, unlike many other everyday "一+X" words that have fully lexicalized the tone-sandhi shift (一定 yídìng, "certainly"; 一样 yíyàng, "same") — a reminder that pinyin tone-sandhi rules have real, dictionary-listed exceptions.

components.note: 力 (strength/force) — 动 relates to movement produced by exertion or force.
亻 (person) plus 乍 (suddenly/for the first time) — together suggesting a person making or doing something for the first time.

example.hanzi: 这个舞蹈的动作很难。
example.pinyin: Zhège wǔdǎo de dòngzuò hěn nán.
example.english: The movements in this dance are very difficult.
example.fact: 动作 names a discrete, often visible physical movement or gesture — a dance move, a martial-arts strike — while the more abstract 行动 ("action, to take action") describes a broader course of action; 动作片 specifically labels the action-movie genre.

components.note: 心 (heart/mind) — 意 relates to thought, intention, and meaning, things of the mind.
音 (yīn) is the historical phonetic element; its modern reading has drifted from yì, though both share a similar vowel.
口 (mouth) — 味 relates to taste, sensed in the mouth.
未 (wèi) gives the sound — an exact match with 味.

example.hanzi: 他的沉默并不意味着他同意。
example.pinyin: Tā de chénmò bìng bú yìwèizhe tā tóngyì.
example.english: His silence doesn't necessarily mean that he agrees.
example.fact: The 着 attached after 意味 casts the verb as an ongoing state of signification, "carries the meaning of" — the same grammatical 着 that marks continuous action elsewhere (吃着, "eating"), here applied to an abstract logical relationship instead of a physical activity.

components.note: 爫 (a hand, from above) — 受 pictures something being passed.
又 (a hand, from below) — one hand giving and another receiving gave 受 its meaning 'to receive' or 'to endure.'
至 (zhì, to arrive) — carries 到's core meaning, 'to reach, to arrive'
刂 (a form of 刀, dāo) gives a sound close to 到's pronunciation dào

example.hanzi: 这部电影受到了观众的欢迎。
example.pinyin: Zhè bù diànyǐng shòudàole guānzhòng de huānyíng.
example.english: This movie was well received by audiences.
example.fact: 受到 is one of Mandarin's most common ways to build a passive-like sentence without the marker 被 — 受到欢迎 ("to be well received") and 受到影响 ("to be affected") both cast the subject as the recipient of some noun-form action, a smoother alternative to a literal 被-passive.

components.note: A stylized foot (related to 止, 'to stop/foot') — originally meant 'to go,' later grammaticalized into a literary possessive/linking particle, similar to 的.
A single horizontal stroke — the simplest possible way to represent the number one; some traditional interpretations link it to heaven or earth as the very first stroke of creation.

example.hanzi: 长城是世界七大奇迹之一。
example.pinyin: Chángchéng shì shìjiè qī dà qíjì zhīyī.
example.english: The Great Wall is one of the world's seven great wonders.
example.fact: 之一 always trails at the very end of its noun phrase (X之一, "one of X") rather than leading it the way English "one of" does — 之 is a literary, classical-Chinese linking particle that survives today mainly in set written-register phrases like this one, alongside 之前 ("before") and 百分之 ("percent").

components.note: ⺮ (bamboo) — ancient texts were written on bound bamboo strips, and 第 originally referred to the sequential order of such strips, giving rise to its meaning 'ordinal number' (as in 第一, first).
三 is made of three simple horizontal strokes stacked together — the most direct way to picture the number three, following the same pattern as 一 (one) and 二 (two).

example.hanzi: 他在班里排名第三。
example.pinyin: Tā zài bān lǐ páimíng dìsān.
example.english: He ranks third in his class.
example.fact: 第 turns a bare cardinal number into an ordinal — 三 alone just means "three," while 第三 means "third" — and the same 第 prefix works uniformly across the entire number system (第一, 第二, 第三 ... 第一百), unlike English's irregular ordinals ("two" becoming "second").

components.note: 面 was originally a pictograph of a human face, with an outline around an eye — later broadening to mean 'face, surface, side.'
又 (hand) and 寸 (also derived from a hand shape) — together suggesting two hands matching or corresponding, related to 对's meaning 'correct, matching.'

example.hanzi: 我们必须面对现实。
example.pinyin: Wǒmen bìxū miànduì xiànshí.
example.english: We must face reality.
example.fact: 面对 literally means "to turn one's face toward" (面 "face" + 对 "toward, facing") — used both for physically facing something and, more often in everyday speech, for confronting an abstract difficulty, the same metaphorical stretch English makes when it says someone must "face" a problem.

components.note: 忄 (heart) — 怀 relates to feelings held close to the heart
不 (bù) gives a sound distantly related to 怀's reading huái, having drifted apart over time
疋 — a person walking, shown pausing and looking back uncertainly
矢 (an arrow/cane) — an old man's walking stick, held while hesitating

example.hanzi: 我怀疑他说的是不是真的。
example.pinyin: Wǒ huáiyí tā shuō de shì bu shì zhēn de.
example.english: I doubt whether what he said is true.
example.fact: 怀疑 covers both English "to doubt" (uncertain something is true) and "to suspect" (believing something bad may be true) in a single word — its first half, 怀, literally means "to hold in one's bosom," an old image of carrying an unresolved feeling close to the chest.

components.note: 户 (door) — 居 relates to where one lives, behind a door
古 (gǔ) gives a sound related to 居's reading jū, from an older, closer pronunciation link
灬 (fire) — 然 originally described burning; the meaning later shifted to 'so, correct' as 然 became a grammatical particle.
肰 (rán) gives the sound — 然 is also pronounced rán, an exact match.

example.hanzi: 他居然一个人爬上了那座山。
example.pinyin: Tā jūrán yí gè rén páshàngle nà zuò shān.
example.english: Surprisingly, he climbed that mountain all by himself.
example.fact: 居然 explicitly colors a sentence with the speaker's own surprise at an unexpected outcome, in the same family as the slightly more formal near-synonym 竟然 — a coloring English usually has to add separately with a word like "surprisingly," rather than baking it into the main verb's neighborhood.
